page_title: A BitTorrent client in Python 3.5 - Markus Eliasson

summary.title: A BitTorrent client in Python 3.5
summary.one_liner: You learn how the BitTorrent protocol works (torrent parsing, tracker announces, peer handshakes, pieces and blocks) and how a small asyncio-based client implements it in Python 3.5.
takeaways: A .torrent file is bencoded metadata; the pieces.bencoding module shows how to decode and encode its four data types in Python.
A tracker returns a compact binary list of peers (4-byte IP plus 2-byte port) in response to an HTTP announce request containing info_hash, peer_id and transfer stats.
Peers exchange length-prefixed messages (Handshake, BitField, Interested, Unchoke, Request, Piece, Have, KeepAlive) over TCP, parsed with struct and an async iterator.
Pieces are subdivided into blocks of 2^14 bytes, which are the units actually requested between peers; the last piece and block may be smaller.
Using asyncio lets a client wait on tracker HTTP calls and many peer connections concurrently without blocking.
summary.summary: The article walks through the BitTorrent protocol and the implementation of "Pieces", an open-source (Apache 2) BitTorrent client built on Python 3.5's asyncio. It covers parsing .torrent metadata with a bencoding decoder, building tracker announce requests and reading the compact peer list, and coordinating peer connections with a work queue and an announce loop. It then explains the peer wire protocol (handshake, bitfield, choke/unchoke, interested, request/piece, have, keepalive), how messages are framed and decoded with struct, and how pieces are split into 16 KiB blocks. The author recommends the Unofficial BitTorrent Specification as the main reference.
